utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84bis-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Can the accused understand and hear the proceedings in the language they understand, Mr. Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARADINAJ
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BALAJ
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Can we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. Paul Rogers, together with Ms. Daniela Kravetz, Mr. Aditya Menon, and our case manager today Mr. Colin Nawrot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Please, Your Honours, I appear on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj together with my learned friends Mr. Rod Dixon, Ms. Annie O'Reilly, and Mr. Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Gregor Guy-Smith, appearing with Colleen Rohan, Chad Mair, Gentian Zyberi on behalf of Idriz Balaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for Mr. Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Richard Harvey, together with me Mr. Paul Troop, there's Sophie Rigney who is our case manager, Mr. Luke Boenisch who will be taking over from her as case manager, and that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harvey. I presume this is the first time that we're sitting as a full Bench. If we have before, I don't think it makes any difference if I re-introduce the Judges with me. On my right I have got Judge Hall and on my left Judge Delvoie. I guess I am known already, having been with you for some time. Just to remind the parties that by order of the President of the 21st of July 2010, this Trial Chamber was assigned to this case for a re-trial. Now today we are having a Pre-Trial Conference, and pursuant to Rule 73 bis the Trial Chamber is required to convene a Pre-Trial Conference prior to the commencement of the trial, and in the course of the Pre-Trial Conference, having heard the Prosecution, the Chamber may determine the number of witnesses the Prosecution may call, the time available to the Prosecution for presenting evidence, and further the Chamber may call upon the Prosecution to shorten the estimated length of the examination-in-chief for some witnesses and fix a number of crime sites or incidents in respect of which evidence may be presented by the Prosecution. Now, at the Status Conference on the 9th of June, 2011, we confirmed that in accordance with Appeals Chamber decisions of the 31st of May, 2011, the operative indictment in this case is the indictment filed by the Prosecution on the 21st of January, 2011. We have also indicated that the Chamber will not invite the Prosecution to reduce the indictment any further. Are we agreed on that? Mr. Rogers, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. I presume also -- Mr. Harvey, I see you nodding, and I will record the nod of Mr. Guy-Smith as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Now, the next item I would like to deal with then is the list of witnesses and estimated time for the presentation of the Prosecution case. On the 3rd of December, 2010, the Prosecution filed its pre-trial brief pursuant to Rule 65 ter (E) together with a witness list and an exhibit list. The Prosecution indicated that it intends to call a total of 57 witnesses and estimated that the total time for its case in chief would be 36.5 hours. However, on the 20th of June, 2011, in accordance with the Chamber's order made at the Status Conference on the 9th of June, 2011, the Prosecution filed a revised pre-trial brief. It indicated that it no longer intended to call one witness and I'm not -- I might not be able to pronounce the name of this witness, Ms. Stephanie Schwandner-Sievers so that the total number of witnesses on the Prosecution's list is now 56. On the 27th of June, the Prosecution filed a motion pursuant to Rule 89(F) of the Rules seeking the admission of the evidence of eight witnesses, a motion pursuant to Rule 92 bis with respect to 14 witnesses, and a motion pursuant to Rule 92 ter with respect to eight witnesses. And on the same day the parties filed a joint motion for admission of agreed evidence which we will address later in this hearing. On the 22nd of July, the Chamber issued its decision on the Prosecution motion pursuant to Rule 92 bis, requiring that two of the proposed witnesses give evidence viva voce to appear for cross-examination and granting in principle the motion with respect to the remaining witnesses. The Chamber will issue decisions on the Prosecution's motions pursuant to Rule 89(F) and Rule 92 ter in due course. We can indicate today that the decision pursuant to Rule 92 ter should be expected in the course of this week. Mr. Rogers, are you in a position to provide revised estimates for the case in chief for the Prosecution in the light of the above developments?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we can reduce the amount of time we will need with Mr. Stijovic and Mr. Zyrapi. I don't think we will require as much as we have indicated. I think we may have indicated as much already to the Chamber. So we can reduce that down. But apart from that, I don't think we can trim anything more off of the case as we have already indicated. It's, if I may say, with respect, Your Honours, it is already a fairly trim case. We've done everything we can to give reasonable and modest time estimates, understanding how some of the witnesses may develop. It may be a little more time will be required with some of them and less with others. And that may be the give and take in the court proceedings, but I really have done my best to make it as short as we can. Apart from those two, I don't see any real reduction in the Prosecution time that I can offer to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers. Mr. Emmerson, any comments from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, save this that we have been in discussions, that's to say the Defence and the Prosecution, during the course of this morning just before Your Honours came into court, and it is likely, I will say no more at this stage, that some of the witnesses in relation to whom it is currently anticipated that they will attend to give evidence live will no longer be required to give evidence live. Can I leave it in that way; in other words, the witness list may in fact shorten, that's shortened by agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is very grateful to you, Mr. Emmerson and while you're standing, may I just mention something that I was remiss of, congratulations on your appointment as the Rapporteur -- United Nations Rapporteur on Terrorism. My -- have I got it partly correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I hope your obligations with them will not sort of interfere with your job with here.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And vice versa indeed. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was an accurate statement as to where we stand right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It was indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then that completes the item on the witness list. The next item is disclosure. Now, at the Status Conference on the 9th of June, 2011, you also confirmed that there were no outstanding issues regarding disclosure pursuant to Rule 66(A) and (B) and 68 at that time. Is there anything that the parties wish to raise in relation to disclosure? Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers. We will hear you at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The only other matter, Your Honour, of course, is the material which remains to be disclosed to the Defence pursuant to the delayed disclosure orders of the Chamber, but apart from that, as far as -- that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Any comments from the Defence? Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an accurate statement of the position as it stands at the moment. It is likely, though, consistent with the Prosecution's duty of continuing review, that there will be further requests for disclosure, in particular in relation to Witness 81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to Witness 81, as I understand the present state of affairs the Prosecution has launched another ex parte request. There has not been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you know of this ex parte request?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because Mr. Rogers had just so indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There has been further delayed disclosure with regard to this witness. It's my understanding that the disclosure obligations as regard Witness 81 should have been completed by this time, and I don't know whether there's been an order issued with regard to any subsequent delayed disclosure requests by Mr. Rogers or not. It's my position that whatever disclosures exist for Mr. -- from Mr. Rogers with regard to Witness 81 should be in our hands at this time pursuant to previous rulings by this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were not asking the Chamber to tell you whether or not it has or has not been issued. You were just wondering if it has been issued, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you know me well enough to know that I'm always curious as to what the state of affairs is, but I'm not making -- I'm not asking -- I'm asking the Chamber not to go outside of its own rules and regulations. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know me very well that I always try to curtail your curiosity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, indeed so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, only subject to materials received today which I may have a further disclosure request on, there is nothing else outstanding. Everything else that has been said to Your Honours reflects the position as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you very well, there is some material that you received today and you might have further request on disclosure on that matter? Do you want to make that request now or are you able to make it at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I will make it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That being the case then, does that dispose of that item? No further comments on that. The next item relates to agreed facts. On the 19th of November, 2010, the parties filed a joint submission on the existence of an armed conflict in Kosovo and only the 27th of June, 2011, the parties filed a joint motion for admission of agreed evidence. Are there any matters in respect of which the parties have been able to reach an agreement since that submission? Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no further developments in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Emmerson, any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the position is that on the 11th of November the Defence on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj served proposed agreed facts running to 89. We are yet to hear a response from the Prosecution. So the ball is very firmly in Mr. Roger's court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will revert to Mr. Rogers soon. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that we have similarly sent to the Prosecution proposed agreed facts from which we have not received any response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, any response to those two comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We couldn't agree to the agreed facts that were submitted because we didn't agree to them and there is no further state that we can take. Now, it may be that we can discuss matters further, but in the light of the admission of evidence relating to both the armed conflict and also relating to the underlying materials concerning the forensic, it perhaps is rather redundant that we now seek to reach agreement on agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I understand the two Defence lawyers, they were at least respecting a response from you, even if to say, sorry, I can't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me, I think I did respond at the time to say that we weren't able to agree those agreed facts because we, at that time if Your Honour remembers, we were trying to deal with the armed conflict issue, and the only thing that came out of our exchange of proposals was the one agreed fact relating to the armed conflict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, I understand that. Mr. Emmerson, did I misquote you? I thought you said we are yet to hear from the Prosecution about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I recall the answer that we received was that while the scope of the re-trial remained the subject of dispute before the Appeals Chamber, the Prosecution was not at that point in a position to respond, bearing in mind that these proposals were put forward in November 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the scope of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Has now been resolved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I would, with respect, invite Mr. Rogers to revisit the issue because the vast majority of the proposed agreed facts are drawn verbatim from the judgement of the Trial Chamber in the original trial, and it really does seem a little difficult to understand why the Prosecution would have a problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just make this caveat. This is a re-trial de novo.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As if there was never a trial before. So this Trial Chamber is not going -- is not going to live in the shadow of the original trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- if you want to propose agreed facts to your opposite number you may do so in the course of your job; however, not linked to the fact that they come from the original trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, well just to be clear, of course we all entirely understand that the Bench will approach the issues in this trial afresh and de novo. But that being said, obviously the more the parties are in a position to narrow the issues in dispute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked not to overlap for the purposes of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- by reference to uncontentious findings of the previous Trial Chamber, presumably the better for more -- the position of all the parties and since there are a vast number of findings of the original Trial Chamber which don't in any way impinge on the issues that are in dispute between the parties in this re-trial and therefore in way encroach upon the independence of this Trial Chamber to reach findings de novo, the extent to which it would be of assistance to refer back to the previous Trial Chamber judgement as part of an agreed facts approach, obviously has the capacity simply for reducing the scope for unnecessary evidence and argumentation and re-find these facts in relation to issues that are not properly in dispute in this re-trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just apologise to the interpreters. It was my fault. I will not do it again. I hear perfectly what you say, Mr. Emmerson, and I can see the practicality of your suggestion. What I just am sort of trying to emphasize is for this trial to be perceived as if it's a step-child of the original child. Things might have been said in the original trial, things might have been adjudicated in the original trial. If the parties are still disputing those things, I think the parties are entitled to dispute them here because this trial is going ahead as if no trial ever took place. If, however, by virtue of issues that were covered whilst in that trial the parties are able to come together and have their minds meet, so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- feel confident that we are approaching the scope and approach of the re-trial from precisely the same perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just taking in mind the discussion you just had with Mr. Emmerson, specifically I would agree with what Mr. Emmerson has said and I understand precisely the Chamber's position. I would point out that the matters -- some of the matters that we are discussing are matters that were not appealed by either party, and with regard to those issues, they are then final judgements and final findings of facts. So to that extent, to the extent it can be of assistance to this Chamber since in fact these are not matters of dispute, it would seem -- it would seem that it would make some sense in that specific limited regard to take not necessarily a total moment from but in a certain sense take certain guidance from that which is no longer part of this particular re-trial. There are a number of facts that exist which are pretty plainly understood and have been plainly dealt with previously that we are attempting to seek agreement. Nothing more, nothing less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, let me just say this, I perfectly accept that some issues may not have been appealed and therefore they are res judicata and that therefore they are facts. However, this Tribunal has a mechanism for presenting that kind of -- those kind of facts to the Court and they come by way of adjudicated facts. If there is no agreement -- the fact that matters have been finalised in court doesn't mean necessarily that all parties agree with the finding and if the other party says, I'm sorry, I can't let those facts come in by way of agreement you have a remedy, sir, by way of adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I most certainly appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the fact that they have not been appealed doesn't mean that everybody agrees on those facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely understood, and we are in total agreement with the state of the law in this regard. But the hope, of course, is that the Prosecution will be reasonable with us here so that we can focus on the issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will not comment on the reasonableness of either party. I believe that all are -- all people here are reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One would hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One would hope. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm reasonably in agreement with that, thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I appreciate your reasonableness, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before Your Honour returns to Mr. Rogers, perhaps rather clumsily, what I was seeking to indicate at the outset is that before the Defence are in a position to evaluate the necessity for a motion on adjudicated facts we have to have a categorical response from the Prosecution as to whether those facts upon which the previous Trial Chamber adjudicated and which are put forward for the purposes of agreement as agreed facts in a document served upon them some nine months ago, whether in the light of the scope of the trial as it now is, they are in a position to agree those facts; that is to say, those that are directly sourced, lifted verbatim from the original trial judgement or whether it's necessary for us to place before this Trial Chamber Trial Chamber adjudicated facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand you perfectly, Mr. Emmerson, thank you so much, which is why I asked Mr. Rogers if he has at least favoured you with the courtesy of a response even if to say I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So I would -- at this stage, now that we know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will go back to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now that we know the scope of the re-trial, I'd simply put down a marker to say this: We would invite the Prosecution to reconsider and confirm what their position is in respect of the particular agreed facts put forward rather than to treat them compendiously, to look at them individually, those that are sourced in the original Trial Chamber judgement, to take a view in relation to it, and to make that clear, let us say within seven days. Thereafter, if it remains necessary to do so, we will file a motion for adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Rogers, do you have any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, one of the difficulties in this particular case has been the three defendants approach things - and I don't mean this critically - approach things from different angles, and what one might agree the others may not, and it really needs to be something from all three defendants that is capable of agreement, otherwise the Court will have to litigate it anyway. So it seems to me sensible for the three accused' representatives to put their heads together, come up with a set of agreed facts that they are all capable of agreeing, because otherwise no point with me agreeing it with one if the other two won't agree it, and then advance their joint agreed facts document to me and then I will look at it. This has been, with respect to my learned friends, and again it's not a criticism, as I understand the particular difficulties of litigating from the Defence perspective, they have to really try to reach an agreement between themselves to put forward the materials that we are capable or may be capable of agreeing and then we can take it from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, simply this: I understand Mr. Rogers' plea for tidiness. There are in reality three sets of agreed facts put forward by the three accused, but as far as I understand it there is unlikely to be the slightest dispute between us, and we would undertake, therefore, by the close of business today, unless anybody dissents, to indicate to Mr. Rogers that the three separate documents can be treated by him as a compendious document and we would invite a response as I said within seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I concur.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In full agreement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's where we stand, Mr. Rogers, and you will perhaps -- might have to give a response to your colleagues the best way you will receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I will and I'm very grateful for the agreement that was reached very swiftly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Okay. That disposes the question about agreed facts. Can we now deal with the guide-lines that were circulated to the parties. Now, on the 22nd of July, 2010, the Chamber circulated - is it 2010 or 2011? - through its Legal Officer proposal for guide-lines on notice and presentation of evidence and invite the parties to comment on the guide-lines. The three Defence teams responded on the 15th of August, the Prosecution on the 16th. The three Defence teams objected to the proposed requirement for a 24 hour notice of documents to be used in cross-examination, that's paragraph 3 of the proposed guide-lines. The Balaj Defence raises objections in particular to paragraph 8 of the guide-lines according to which a party cross-examining a Rule 92 bis witness shall limit its cross-examination to the matters in respect of which cross-examination has been ordered. The Chamber does note the two rules or sub-rules that the Balaj Defence refers to. I personally seem to understand 90(H)(i), but I'm not quite sure 90 bis (C) how it operates, but I'll re-study it. And the Balaj Defence also proposes a new rule according to which second degree or multiple hearsay evidence is inadmissible. The Prosecution opposes this proposal. And the Brahimaj Defence seeks confirmation in relation to paragraph 10 of the proposed guide-lines to the effect that cross-examination of a Rule 92 ter witness falls into the category allowing for the time for cross-examination to exceed the time for examination-in-chief. Have I captured the stand of the parties accurately? Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour has, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You confirm, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I don't know whether Your Honour wishes to hear submissions in relation to point 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will -- we will come to that. I just wanted to know have I captured it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you confirm that too?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you too, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Point 3, I think I can take the Defence point on that point and I believe, my fellow Judges also do. However, what is good for the goose is good for the gander. You will at some stage or you might at some stage lead evidence and the Prosecution might have to cross-examination, it will also be the same rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Precisely, I would expect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, would you like us to amend the guide-line to say you give notice of your exhibits at the beginning of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think there were two different ways in which this problem has been resolved in different trials. One is to say after examination-in-chief has begun and the other is to say at the moment of the beginning of cross-examination. Logically it really ought to be the latter if the aim of postponing disclosure is to be properly maintained. In other words, so that the Prosecution -- I mean, it may seem a little fanciful, but it is not entirely beyond the bounds of possibility that a Prosecutor alight to the documents that are likely to be put in cross-examination would materially alter the scope of examination-in-chief in order to anticipatorily deal with those matters. And since the purpose of a delayed disclosure is to allow cross-examination to be at its most effective in order to give the Trial Chamber the best possible impression of seeing a witness's response when first confronted unexpectedly with the document, it would seem that the logical solution should be at the moment cross-examination begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that was in fact your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think different proposals have been put forward. That is our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] And I would imagine that your submission would actually cover the proposals of the other two Defence teams because the other two Defence teams it gives them a little bit of leeway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. But my submission is immediately before cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm with Mr. Guy-Smith on that proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any comments, Mr. Rogers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mr. Emmerson's original position of course was that he was content for disclosure at the beginning of examination-in-chief for the reasons that he said primarily the concern is that one would pre-prepare a witness during the course of proofing to deal with the documents, and as such once the witness is sworn that wouldn't be possible, and therefore there is no objection from him at that point in time for it to be disclosed at the start of examination-in-chief. Your Honours, we would -- we would prefer the 24 hours because it does give us an opportunity to look at the documents, to identify any rebuttal material that there may be, and for us to prepare ourselves to deal with the witness and to deal with any answers or to consider or to think about the re-examination that we may wish to undertake with the witnesses. The suggestion of not allowing us to see them earlier is really is suggesting that we would try to do something improper with the witness. I don't think my learned friends want to put that so strongly, but really that's what's sitting underneath their concern. Your Honours, so we would prefer the original view of the Chamber for 24 hours' notice because it does assist us to prepare the case effectively to deal with any matters that arise. If not, then we would prefer again for it to be at the beginning of examination-in-chief, which again gives us a little more time to try to find the materials, look at the documents. Your Honours, can I say one of the particular difficulties here is the nature of much of this evidence is likely to be 92 ter and really there won't be any examination-in-chief, and so the documents will arrive, examination-in-chief will be over, and during the course of the cross-examination one's having to not only listen to the answers but look at the documents and try to look into them to see if there is any other material which may rebut or may provide an alternative explanation to the material that's identified. And my learned friends know perfectly well that in cases of this size with a huge amount of documentation that exists, that takes an amount of time for both sides to do in fairness. And, Your Honour, I think if it's provided too late, the risk is witnesses end up being re-called in order to deal with new material that's just been discovered that if one had had sufficient notice one would have been able to deal with in evidence when the witness was before the Court. I think it depends a little on how one views the adversarial process or the process that the Court is adopting. If one's looking at it as an opportunity to try to establish the full picture from the witness, then there really is no objection to notice being given to the Prosecutor of the material that intends to be used. If one is looking at it perhaps in a more challenging way, then the traditional common law approach of rabbits out of hats and startling opportunities for witnesses may be more favourable. Your Honour, I think in the more mature system one is looking at more maximum notice, and I would ask for as much notice as the court considers appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I respond very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, it had never been the position of the Haradinaj Defence that the beginning of examination-in-chief was preferable, it was simply the submission in the e-mail that was sent to the Court that that was the position that had been adopted by previous Trial Chamber trying this case. And as Your Honour rightly pointed out, this is not the step-child of the previous trial, but that being said Mr. Rogers' suggestion that this is a case where there's likely to be a large amount of 92 ter evidence and therefore no examination-in-chief rather undercuts the proposition that the time-frame should be the beginning of examination-in-chief rather than cross-examination because if he's right that there's not going to be any examination-in-chief those two will collapse into one and the same. And finally this, when this matter was discussed in the previous trial, it was discussed in writing, the detailed motion, in which both parties explained their respective positions rather like Mr. Rogers has just sought to do on the back of an envelope by suggesting that there is something immature about trial by ambush or pulling rabbits out of hats and to which the Defence responded in writing at some length examining the history and value of cross-examination to the adversarial trial process. These are adversarial proceedings and it's long been recognised in all jurisdictions which adopt adversarial proceedings that getting at the truth is very often most effectively achieved by seeing a witness's first reaction when confronted. Now, it's wrong to suggest that for us to insist on disclosure at that moment, in other words, at a time when it could not materially affect the witness's prior testimony, somehow implies impropriety on the part of the Prosecution, because were Mr. Rogers to get what he seeks, which is 24 hours' notice of the very issues that are going to be put to confront and challenge these three key witnesses, there would be nothing improper in him using that material in a proofing session in forewarning the witness and asking for their comments on the material which is likely to be put to them in cross-examination. It wouldn't be coaching, it would be asking for their prior response and thereby depriving the Trial Chamber of the very tool that it most accurately and acutely needs in assessing whether they're telling the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any further comments, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I recently finished a trial -- I recently finished a trial which I believe that you were intimately involved in. This was a procedure that we used. The documents that were involved in that case are vastly greater than the documents that will be involved in this case, the magnitude, the sheer magnitude of paper. And if the Chamber may recall, nary a witness was recalled, not one witness was recalled as a result of this particular procedure being used in that case. It was sauce for the goose and for the gander. It worked efficiently, it worked expeditiously, and I see no reason for it not to be used again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what was that procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That procedure was immediately before cross-examination. That was the procedure that I submitted in the proposed modification that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey, do you have any final word on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Nothing to add, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess on this issue specifically the Chamber will reserve its decision and will confer and will come back to the parties about it okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I just raise one matter about the scope of 92 ter in particular because it may impact upon Your Honours' decision. Your Honour, our understanding is that the Tribunal's and Chambers in this particular Tribunal do permit some scope for examination-in-chief even with a 92 ter witness beyond merely reading out the summary. And I was just going to raise, it may be a convenient moment to deal with it, Your Honours' understanding of how paragraph 7 would work in practice because on one view it would appear that the only thing that could be dealt with during the course of 92 ter evidence would be the reading out of the summary, but clearly when one is tendering documents through a witness - and I have in mind in particular Mr. Zyrapi, it would take a while to go through those documents with the individual to tender them into evidence. And I'm anticipating that Your Honour would be permitting a certain amount of scope for examination-in-chief even with a 92 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- witness to clarify any matters, a certain amount of settling is normal with witnesses who have just come into the witness box, and then to deal with any documents that need to be produced through the witness. That's my understanding of how the Chamber is likely to proceed. If I might just confirm that's the case. And if not, what Your Honours' views would be so that we can modify our procedures accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say you might just confirm, or do you want the Chamber to confirm for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, please. If you might just confirm for me, that is you, the Chamber, might just confirm for me my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine that that would be so said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Particularly where there are a number of exhibits to be tendered in because they would have to be tendered in one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, if I'm right with regard to the specific issue at hand, I believe that the testimony of at least one witness who the Prosecution intends to introduce by way of 92 ter is a situation in which the witness has already been extensively examined about each and every document that is part of their 92 ter statement. If such is the case, then there will be no reason for there to be any further clarification or examination on those documents because it had already been done in a previous proceeding and/or through previous statements, where the explanation had been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand what you mean by previous proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, in the previous trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith, I've got to repeat that. We are not in the shadow of the previous trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber must determine independently the admissibility of every exhibit that is tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's not what I'm suggesting, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting is, as we both know, a 92 ter witness takes the stand, the questions are asked of that 92 ter witness, which is: Will you -- do you adopt the statement that you made previously?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Statement, not proceeding, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Statement. In this situation it would be a statement under oath. In this situation what you have is you have a witness who has been previously shown an exhibit, which is now part and parcel of that 92 ter statement, which he is now once again adopting, and when the admission is brought by the Prosecution, they will be admitting wholesale, I would think, and perhaps I'm incorrect, they will be admitting wholesale all of those exhibits that were previously the subject matter of this particular witness's testimony and/or statement, however you wish to characterise it. Therefore, the notion that there will be further explanation with regard to those exhibits means in essence that the witness is a viva voce witness and not a 92 ter witness, and there is a distinction between the two and the reason that we have the 92 ter rule is to expedite proceedings. If the Prosecution wishes to call the witness as a viva voce witness, then they should do so. If they're using the 92 ter procedure which has happened often, hopefully will not happen in this particular trial, as a manner to get around the viva voce time concerns, that should not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- before you speak, may I just reassure Mr. Guy-Smith that it's not our intention to go through all of the exhibits all over again. It's to deal with the new material that we have identified on the 65 ter exhibit list. One of the dangers I think of dealing with things in abstracto, as we sort of are a little bit, is that perhaps we can become concerned about matters that actually aren't going to happen in reality. I was simply seeking some general understanding of Your Honours' views about how to deal with 92 ter, and I was expecting that we might deal with any specific objections as and when the witnesses came to testify. But if it helps Mr. Guy-Smith, I can tell him that that's -- we don't intend to abuse Rule 92 ter to get around the viva voce time-limits because we've already shrunk our case to 36 hours and I'm not sure it would be of much use trying to do that. So I hope that's some reassurance to him that we don't intend to do what he thinks we might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you just took the words out of my mouth. I was going to say to Mr. Guy-Smith that we will deal with these issues as and when they arise as we go along because right now, as you rightly say, we are just arguing in the air and we don't have a concrete problem for us that we need to solve. I would imagine that as we go along the Chamber will rule in the interests of justice on how to deal with each situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate, Your Honour, but as a matter of fact we do have a concrete problem because we have not received 92 ter statements from some of these proposed witnesses with regard to the - as Mr. Rogers has put it - the new evidence, so we don't know what the new evidence is that he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's only reason why we can't even begin to talk. Let's talk when we have the new evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just make one observation which perhaps can be made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- in principle, and it may seem an obvious one but since we're in the business of setting out what our understanding of the procedure is likely to be in view of the very unusual circumstances in which this trial comes to be conducted, and of course mindful of the fact that we are not a step-child, nonetheless with those witnesses who are brought by the Prosecution for a second time in order to give supplementary evidence, it is certainly my understanding of the most efficient and ordinarily conduct of these proceedings that since the Prosecution have also sought to introduce via 92 ter the transcripts of the evidence that the witnesses gave, including cross-examination at the original trial as part of their testimony, that it would be unnecessary as a duplication of effort and expense for cross-examination to be repeated on the same topics; in other words, it would not be my intention to re-cross-examine any witness who gave evidence at the original trial on the topics or in the manner that I cross-examined him at the original trial, instead relying and standing upon the cross-examination and answers given at the trial number one. Failing that, otherwise you'll simply be re-hearing cross-examination that's already been dealt with. Obviously if there's new material that the witness is now being called to produce, then cross-examination may be directed to the new material, but in truth that's the only fresh evidence being put before this Trial Chamber. That same witness will then be adopting the evidence that they gave at the previous trial, which of course includes the evidence that they gave under cross-examination. And so if I can just put it bluntly -- I mean, to take an example, there is one witness who is going to be giving evidence before you about the production of intelligence documents by the Serbian intelligence services. At the original trial under cross-examination he acknowledged that the statements had been obtained through a combination of torture, blackmail, and bribery. I don't propose to re-traverse that general methodology. It is there on the transcript for all to see. And so if I can indicate that my general approach will be simply to adopt the cross-examination and evidence given in answer to cross-examination at the original trial in respect of evidence given at the original trial and to confine my cross-examination in the interests of efficiency and in the interests of justice to any new matters that the witness might now be being called to testify about over and above that which they were called to testify about at the original trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just say before Mr. Guy-Smith stands up that I appreciate what you say; however, with the caveat that I put earlier that we are not in the shadow of the previous trial, I do not think it is for the Chamber to comment on how the Defence must conduct its case. But as I say, I appreciate the fact that you are contributing towards the expeditiousness of the trial, and to that extent I'm very grateful and I'm sure the Chamber is. But you are not limited in what questions you would like to ask as a cross-examiner within the bounds of the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that. But it could -- just to tease this out just a little further, there could possibly be a misunderstanding as between Your Honour and myself. I will treat questions asked and answers given at the original trial which are being admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter with equal evidential status and weight as a question and answer put to the witness in these proceedings. And on that understanding, I hope it will be possible to proceed expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Certainly if a transcript is admitted, that will be taken as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that indeed was the point that I was apparently inartfully - and I apologise for that - trying to make when I initially started this particular journey with you. The issue of whether or not it is appropriate for new evidence to come through a 92 ter witness is presently the subject matter of a pending motion and I will leave it at that for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey, everybody has had his part of the cherry, you don't want to take yours? Okay. As I did say -- are we still on that point, we're still on 3, guide-line 3, the Chamber will decide that and will provide a new guide-line or stick with what we have depending on what we decide. Mr. Guy-Smith, in your objections to paragraph 8, you said you don't want to be limited to the issues raised in examine -- obviously, you might want to cross-examine on credibility which may not necessarily be -- have been canvassed in examination-in-chief. I -- within those rules of cross-examination we understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With that understanding, there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Rogers, you take issue with Mr. Guy-Smith's submission on the inadmissibility of double hearsay. I would like you to start with single hearsay. Are you saying -- I understand that at this Tribunal it is admissible. The question of weight is another matter. Can I hear what you have to say or let the Chamber hear what you have to say on the double hearsay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's always the same point. It's about weight and the weight that the Chamber is prepared to give to this form of evidence, and it may be that at the end of the day, having heard all of the evidence, the Chamber attributes to it no weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: At all. But it may be that the Chamber attributes to it some weight. It may depend on the other material that is produced during the course of the trial, and I think, respectfully, to try to produce a blanket exclusion at this stage of the proceedings would be -- would not be right. It would be wrong. It would be better to receive the evidence that is available and for the Court at the end of the day to determine what weight, if any, it gives to that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, do you have any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I actually thought long and hard about this and I attempted to take into consideration the precise concern that Mr. Rogers has raised. And if we are to look at this second sentence that I suggested as a rule here, I suggested multiple hearsay and/or unsourced hearsay is inadmissible in the absence of independent objective corroborative evidence. So that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a standing rule even first-hand hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Single hearsay, if I can use that term. I don't know what term to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that we all appreciate the difficulty with multiple hearsay because the distinction between multiple hearsay or unsourced hearsay and rumour and gossip is unfortunately virtually indistinguishable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In principle how is single hearsay not rumour or gossip?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Single hearsay, very simply this: Single hearsay comes from a position where it's an out of court statement which is made -- offered to prove the truth of matters asserted by -- it could be by a single author. For example, I could say Judge Moloto said to me that Mr. Rogers is not being particularly candid. Now, if I were to say such a thing, and I don't think that you would say such a thing nor do I think that Mr. -- the issue was whether or not Mr. Rogers is particularly candid or not, that certainly wouldn't be an issue of rumour. However -- however, if I were to say: I have heard in the courtroom or I have heard at the Tribunal that Mr. Rogers is not candid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the unsourced --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's the unsourced one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The multiple one. You have heard from Mr. Mair that Judge Moloto said that Mr. Rogers is -- you didn't hear directly from Judge Moloto.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's now the multiple --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's your multiple situation, and in the multiple situation it raises a couple of concerns not the least of which being how do I get to investigate it, how do I counter that. What is the evidentiary value, if any, to a fact-finder? And with regard to the issue of weight versus admissibility, and I appreciate and I have full confidence that the Chamber understands how to do its job and that's really not what I'm going after here, but it seems to me that we run dangerously close to being in a situation where the Prosecution is going to bucket-in rumour and gossip, multiple hearsay, unsourced hearsay with regard to ultimately in this -- with regard to ultimately in this case character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what the basis for that submission is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The disclosure that I have received from the Prosecution and I really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I suggest --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- at this point that as and when that happens you jump up, you jump up and object, and let the Chamber rule on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll be more than happy to do that, but I also think that in a responsible sense with regard to an adversarial process, the notion that unsourced hearsay can be given any credence whatsoever from the standpoint of admissibility is something that should be arrested at the front gate. With regard -- I understand your concerns about multiple hearsay, I take a different view, but I don't think I'm going to be particularly successful in arguing through the multiple hearsay by the way that you are looking at me and the kind of conversation we are having.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are clairvoyant?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, no, I've just -- I've spent a lot of time with you, Your Honour, but I really do believe that with regard to the issue of unsourced hearsay, the dangers of giving it any credence whatsoever far outweigh any utility that it can have to the fact-finder.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just indicate this, the quality of the material that's going to be put before you from, in particular, the witness I adverted to a moment ago from the intelligence services including as it does statements which on their own admission were obtained in the fashion I just described, will, I apprehend, in due course make it entirely clear to Your Honours what it is Mr. Guy-Smith is so anxious about because there will be, and you will see it in due course, just a vast amount of frankly forensic rubbish being put before you in an attempt to create a no-smoke-without-fire-type approach even though the source of it is largely often anonymous and the methodologies by which it has been obtained are amongst the basest for any investigative source in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I assure the parties that the Chamber will make sure that it adheres to rules of evidence, rules of procedure and the rules of this Court to ensure that only credible, probative, relevant evidence is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in effect that is precisely what we would anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in due course you'll see why we're concerned about it because the sort of material that is going to be put to you falls very short of any of those standards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in fact that's why we have you here, to make sure that you can either block it at the first gate, front gate, or at the back gate, or the middle gate, whatever gate -- whatever gate you want --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In the end, I apprehend Your Honours will have no problem blocking it somewhere along the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you so much. You have something to say? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hesitate to say anything more unless Your Honours wish me to, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't necessarily wish you to say anything, but if you have something I don't want to gag you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm happy to be gagged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're happy to be gagged. Mr. Harvey, you don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm happy for him to be gagged as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about you, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're gagging yourself. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I make just one procedural point for the sake of accuracy. I notice on the transcript, page 31, lines 1 to 7, a lengthy submission of Mr. Rogers is attributed to Your Honour as though it were Your Honour's response to a submission. It's quite important that that be qualified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, you are very right. I would hate to take credit for Mr. Rogers' brilliant submissions. Line?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Page 31, lines 1 to 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One to 7. Okay. I guess our stenographer will make note of that. Thank you so much, Mr. Emmerson. Well, then let's leave that point. I need to be reminded, what were we talking about -- oh, the admissibility of hearsay. Maybe the Chamber might confirm for you, Mr. Harvey, that what you asked in relation to paragraph 10, yes, will be taken on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. And I would imagine that that disposes of all the issues that were raised by the parties on this matter? Thank you so much. Item 6 is a joint motion for admission of evidence. On the 27th of June, 2011, the parties filed a joint motion for admission of agreed evidence with confidential annex A and public annex B. Annex A contains a list of transcript -- of testimony of witnesses and/or witness statements from the original case, that is the Haradinaj case, and associated exhibits listed in the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list. Annex B contains a list of additional exhibits not on the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list which the Defence proposes for admission and to which the Prosecution does not object. The Chamber takes note of the content of these documents. It will request the Registry -- the Registry Court Officer, I beg your pardon, to assign a P exhibit number to each document listed in annex A of the joint motion of the 27th of June and a D exhibit number to each document listed in annex B and to notify the parties and the Chambers accordingly. Does that settle it? Mr. Rogers, would that settle it that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, will you please take note of that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, an internal memorandum will be distributed to the parties with the relevant numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Then can we move to item 7, reference to exhibit numbers. It's been brought to the attention of the Chamber that counsel may inadvertently - and I say this with trepidation, I really didn't want to raise this but this is what has been brought to the Chamber's notice. That counsel may inadvertently refer to documents tendered in the present trial by the exhibit number in the original trial which may create confusion. The Chamber would request counsel to pay special attention to this issue and to refer to documents either by their Rule 65 ter number or by the document ID number or by the exhibit number in this case to avoid any possible confusion with documents admitted in the original Haradinaj trial. Is that okay by you, Mr. Rogers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: We will do our very best to avoid the pitfalls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then we move on to opening statements and statements of the accused. Pursuant to Rule 84 of the Rules, before the Prosecution -- the presentation, I beg your pardon, of evidence by the Prosecution each party may make an opening statement. The Defence may, however, elect to make its statement before the presentation of evidence for the Defence. I believe counsel for Haradinaj has indicated informally that it intends to make an opening statement. Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson, for confirming that. Is any other of the Defence teams in a position to indicate whether it would be making an opening statement tomorrow, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is not our intention to be making an opening statement at the outset of these proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Neither is it ours. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Rogers, are you able to give an indication of the length of the opening statement of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I think I'll be a couple of hours in opening the case. I have some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is a couple --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: About two, between two and three, but I think it's nearer to two than three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I shall be less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will be less than an hour. So it could be three and four. Okay. Now, the Rules also provide for the possibility for the accused, if he so wishes, to address the Chamber after the opening statement of the parties or if the Defence elects to defer its opening statement after the opening statement of the Prosecution. Are any of your accused desirous of making some statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. It makes life much easier. Item 9, the availability of the Prosecution witnesses scheduled to testify in the first two weeks of sittings. Mr. Rogers, do you wish to make any submissions on the availability of your witnesses scheduled for the first two weeks of trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll take a break and come back in about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to round off, I wanted to say if I -- and I think I did say it a little earlier, on this point we are just going to have to wait for developments to play themselves out and -- but we are not going to postpone anything or cancel any session, court session. So that if he comes early, we can sit; if he doesn't come early and it's beyond our control, there is nothing we can do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, and plainly there would need to be an application made on his behalf -- I'm sorry, plainly I'm sure Your Honours wouldn't tolerate the tail wagging the dog. There would have to be an application made on his behalf by his counsel for his absence in return -- in response to the subpoena that requires his attendance on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine that everything is going to be done by the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We close the point now on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We were -- we went into open session. That matter is closed. I'm not going to refer to it any longer. Mr. Rogers, we are on the question of the availability of the Prosecution witnesses scheduled for the first week. We have dealt with one. Are you able to tell us any more about the rest?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid we will need to go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I know this may not necessarily be provided for in the Pre-Trial Conference, but it's provided for in the Status Conference. But even before I go to the last item, I just do want to ask the accused to say anything they would like to say about their health and their conditions of detention. Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARADINAJ
utterances.text: Everything okay, Your Honour, health and conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Haradinaj. Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BALAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything, everything is absolutely fine, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing further to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, is there any other matter that any of the parties may wish to raise at this stage? Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Just to raise the issue of Albanian translation. We understand there are very limited translation resources within the Tribunal, and that may cause some difficulties in providing Albanian translations, for example, of proofing notes or that type of material. We will do our best to get those translated as quickly as we can. In terms of providing them to the Defence, as soon as they are available, we will provide them. So they may come on a Sunday evening once they are ready so my learned friends should be aware of that. But as soon as any proofing note is available, it will be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And I don't know whether -- I see Mr. Guy-Smith, but perhaps I can just deal with one other matter which is photographs and maps. Your Honour, we intend to provide the Chamber with a bundle of photographs and maps relevant to the case. They've all been disclosed, they've all been available to the Defence. So I've mentioned that and it may be helpful for you to have those readily available as opposed to keep trying to find them in e-court. Sometimes it's easier to have them there. The only one that isn't there is a map that I will refer to just by way of opening tomorrow which is a map showing the general locations of the area with some of the geographical detail of the main map removed so it's easier to see, and I will show my learned friends it in advance, but that's all it is, it's just an extract, something that we have created to assist I hope. That's all I think I wanted to raise, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Rogers. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I want to take this opportunity to very briefly alert the Chamber once again to the question that is presently pending in regards to both the Balaj and Brahimaj teams with regard to a meeting so that we can appropriately deal with resources. There are some issues that have arisen, and I'm quite mindful of these issues, specifically with regard to the issue of translation and Albanian interpreters because we actually have somewhat of a solution in terms of the limitations of the interpreter services that presently exist. However, we need to have particular resources in order to be able to assist in that solution because we're about to lose one of our team members, but I think this is a matter that can be taken up outside of these proceedings, but I wish to alert the Court to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I'm grasping exactly what you are saying. You are saying because of resources you are losing somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, because of resources I'm losing somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that person is an Albanian-speaking kind of person?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, he's currently volunteering right now. He has been with me since the very first Kosovo case. He is an invaluable resource. He is not only an invaluable resource from the standpoint of his interpretation abilities, he also is a lawyer in his own right and is an individual who has institutional knowledge which is of great assistance not only to my team specifically but to all of the co-accused and has been used in that fashion, but we may be losing him. As a matter of fact I -- at this point I believe we will be losing him unless something can be remedied, but that's something we can deal with away from these proceedings. The other thing I want to raise, and I'm raising this very, very gently and very delicately because it's something that's been repeatedly said at today's proceedings, which is the question of whether or not the Prosecution is bound by that order referring to a previous order. And you had indicated - and it's been said a number of times - that we are not under the shadow of prior proceedings. There is pending litigation which right now is -- exists because of that specific assumption I think that has been between the parties on a number of different occasions, where there have been pre-existing orders made by the Trial Chamber in the first trial that are -- that have been continued in force or have continued to be respected by either the Defence or by the Prosecution with regard to these proceedings. And I wish to just get some clarification because I do not wish to offend at all. But, for example, there's a specific disclosure request that we have and that disclosure request was rejected by the Prosecution based upon a pre-existing order from an original -- from the first Trial Chamber. And I don't want to be arguing back and forth between -- between the two Trial Chambers if that's not the case. So that's why I raise the issue quite gently because this is an area where perhaps -- perhaps Mr. Rogers and I could have some agreement, perhaps not, I don't know. We may still have legal disagreements, but right now part of the argument that is current as an argument, it exists with a pre-existing order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want clarity from the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I -- if I get some kind of just clarifications on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping Speakers] My recollection of the Rules is that the only continuing order that outlives the Chamber from which it came is an order with respect to protective measures. And that one will subsist until ordered, varied, or amended by some other Chamber. Any order that is made in a particular trial for purposes of that trial does not in my interpretation of -- or my understanding of the law, does not bind subsequent Trial Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. I'm clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except for the kind of thing that comes from appeal and it's a jurisprudential thing that ties your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So apart from any issues concerning res judicata or law of the case I understand that. Very well. Thank you very much for that clarification. I do appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Are you done? Thank you so much. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further today. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, there being no further business to conduct, we stand adjourned to the next trial date, tomorrow in the afternoon, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of August, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.40 p.m.,
